Four years of physics at degree level won’t keep you ahead of the field. The syllabus hands you the basics and a peek at the unknown, but tackling the real messy stuff—those complex, bleeding-edge problems—takes obsession and the right crew. You won’t find that in a lecture hall. It’s out there, in the wild, where people wrestle with questions the textbook can’t answer.

Today, though, many students prioritize grades over that deeper pursuit. It’s hard to blame them when jobs and opportunities hinge on academic scores rather than creative thinking. This focus shapes a workforce skilled at maintaining the status quo but less equipped to push boundaries. Over time, it risks leaving us with societies that excel at managing knowledge rather than creating it.

In my country, this is especially clear. Success is tied almost entirely to grades, a single metric that can’t capture a student’s full potential. Those who thrive often do so by mastering the system, not by stretching their abilities. Meanwhile, I’ve seen students who work tirelessly, stumble through setbacks, and grow from every challenge, only to be overlooked because their strengths don’t align with what’s measured. I’ve seen kids grind through failure after failure, learning more than the A-students ever will, only to get branded as failures because their strengths don’t fit the box. Their effort and resilience deserve recognition, but the system rarely sees beyond exam results.

Indeed, today's outcomes are largely shaped by this system. Those who work hard are expected to get what they deserve. However, there are also students who work tirelessly, face repeated failures, and learn extensively, yet their capabilities lie beyond the system’s predefined scope. Unfortunately, this often leads them to be unfairly perceived as lacking intelligence. This highlights the failure of the system to recognize moral desert—what students intrinsically deserve based on their efforts and talents—instead prioritizing institutional desert tied to grades and exams.

Look at the ones who keep going anyway. The ones who fail, dust off, and charge back in. They’ve got guts and gifts the system’s too blind to spot. A real meritocracy wouldn’t just tally points but it’d hunt for that fire, reward the hustle, and match talent to what the world actually needs. Instead, we’ve got a machine that crowns the clever conformists and leaves the innovators in the dirt. That’s not merit. That’s a rigged game. We should aim for a system that celebrates both achievement and the drive to innovate, not just the ability to ace a test.
